source.title: How Optimality Structures Sparse Dictionaries: A Theory for Understanding SAE Representations

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper refines claims about sparse-feature geometry and SAE representations with optimality analyses and experiments. It argues that dictionary-learning objectives impose structure on extracted features and shows that some optimality conditions fail off-distribution.
record.gate_note: The paper tests feature-geometry conditions in toy dictionary-learning settings and evaluates optimality conditions on GPT2-small SAEs. It does not test polysemanticity as a capacity mechanism, whether SAE features recover the model’s complete feature set, or whether superposed features in neural networks are generally one-dimensional.
record.test_reason: The paper gives an analytic argument, with toy checks, that the vanilla dictionary-learning objective itself imposes structure on SAE features. Hierarchical features cannot survive in an optimum, and splitting continues with width (ray-clustering). This bears on whether SAE features are canonical model units (V5). Its GPT2-small experiments measure whether SAEs satisfy necessary optimality conditions, a fit diagnostic rather than a measure of V5. Its toy models are dictionaries, not networks storing features in superposition, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that splitting, absorption, residual structure, dense antipodal pairs and infinite splitting are imposed by the dictionary-learning objective. Real SAEs pass the conditions on training data but fail increasingly on more distant data. They state that whether neural networks use linear superposition remains open.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops first-order and convex analyses of vanilla dictionary learning and tests derived conditions on toy dictionaries and GPT2-small SAEs; it does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Out-of-distribution dataset and layer affect the measured violations; feature activity cutoff and SAE width are also varied for some analyses.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretrained GPT2-small layer-8 SAEs satisfy necessary dictionary-learning optimality conditions on their training distribution. Violations, mostly strict hierarchies, grow with layer distance and on non-English and code data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary-learning optimality conditions diagnose when an SAE's dictionary no longer fits the data it is applied to.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy dictionary learning, feature stability depends on joint activation ranges. Categorical features inactive at least half the time are stable for any dictionary geometry.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which features an optimal sparse dictionary can stably extract depends on the features' joint distribution and sparsity.

record.problems: The authors state that their conditions are necessary rather than sufficient, are derived for vanilla dictionary learning rather than specific encoder architectures, and are tested only pairwise and on subsets of features. The real-SAE experiments use GPT2-small and selected datasets; the joint search is explicitly not exhaustive.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out.

untested.parts: All. No network storing more sparse features than dimensions is studied; the toy models are dictionaries fitted to data.
All. The paper does not test whether LLM activations are spread across neurons or contain recoverable sparse features.
Completeness of SAE features relative to the model's true features, and an empirical comparison of SAE features with model-internal units.

missing.what: Wide-limit ray-clustering result: feature splitting continues with width until each data ray from the optimal bias gets its own atom. Includes a toy check where a 30-neuron dictionary uses only 4 active neurons.
Dense antipodal feature pairs derived as an objective-imposed property for variables active more than half the time, with a simulation check.
Feature-residual condition: hierarchical sub-features are forced into the parent feature's direction rather than left in the residual.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1 links are wrong. The toy settings concern what a dictionary/SAE optimum extracts, not superposition inside a network. The real-SAE rows measure optimality-condition violations, a fit diagnostic, not whether features are canonical units. They are moved to fits_no_version. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test neural networks with more sparse features than dimensions, nor establish that their features are generally nearly orthogonal. It does not test feature importance.
No direct test of neuron polysemanticity as competition for limited capacity, or of important features receiving dedicated dimensions.
No direct test of polysemantic neurons arising for reasons other than superposition.
The paper evaluates SAE optimality conditions, not whether LLM activations are spread across neurons or whether an SAE recovers the model’s underlying sparse features.
The paper tests necessary optimality conditions and their distribution sensitivity, not whether SAE features are complete or canonical units relative to the model’s true representation.
The paper does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features as the units of superposition.

rows.subject: two-element dictionary
rows.operation_detail: Trained dictionaries on three toy datasets while varying feature-direction cosine similarity.
rows.measure: Amodularity index of the resulting representation
rows.note: The text says meaningful amodularity occurs only when predicted by the convex-hull conditions; numeric index values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Measures dictionary-element mixing when fitting toy data, not a network storing sparse features in superposition. No V1 transition or geometry is measured. Figure-only.

rows.subject: dictionary-learning model (mutually exclusive categories)
rows.operation_detail: Derived a condition for a one-hot category representation to satisfy the feature optimality condition.
rows.measure: Condition for stability of one-hot category features
rows.value: The condition is sum over j != k of qj(1 - cos(theta_k,j)) <= 1; with an orthogonal dictionary its left side is 1 - q0 - qk < 1.
rows.note: Analytical result; the paper also says the strict condition persists for orthogonally embedded categories at sufficiently small lambda.
rows.check: Analytic stability condition for a dictionary-learning optimum on categorical data. It concerns the SAE objective, not network superposition (V1).

rows.subject: dictionary-learning model (mutually exclusive categories)
rows.operation_detail: Derived when a one-hot category representation is stable for every dictionary geometry.
rows.measure: Condition for stability across all geometries
rows.value: For equally likely categories, q0 >= (K - 2)/(2(K - 1)); this tends to 1/2 as K grows.
rows.note: Analytical condition linking sparsity to the range of stable geometries.
rows.check: Analytic condition on dictionary stability across geometries. The sparsity threshold concerns the SAE optimum, not the V1 superposition transition.

rows.subject: dictionary-learning model (hierarchically related features)
rows.operation_detail: Applied the necessary feature-feature optimality condition to a lower-level feature that activates only when a higher-level feature is active.

conditions.value: lower-level feature is nested within higher-level feature

rows.measure: Whether the feature pair can be locally optimal
rows.value: The pair is unstable for every cosine similarity except perfect alignment.
rows.note: The paper says feature splitting or absorption can instead make the features mutually exclusive and stable.
rows.check: Analytic result: nested (hierarchical) feature pairs cannot be a dictionary-learning optimum except at perfect alignment. So an optimal dictionary cannot represent such features as given, and splitting or absorption is imposed by the objective. Linked to V5, not V1.

rows.note: The paper reports no violations in sampled sets of up to 100 features either.
rows.check: Count of necessary-optimality violations is an SAE fit diagnostic. Passing does not show features are complete or canonical model units.

relationships.condition: Vanilla dictionary-learning optima (analytic, with toy checks)
relationships.reason: Hierarchical features cannot be an optimum (r4). The text also derives that splitting continues with width toward one atom per data ray (Sec. 7, Fig. 5), so features are objective- and width-dependent, not canonical. The second point is text-based.
relationships.display_finding: Hierarchical features cannot be an optimum, and splitting continues with width toward one atom per data ray, so features depend on objective and width rather than being canonical.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Toy category and two-feature dictionary settings
reader_labels.reason: The results show that feature stability depends on the joint distribution and sparsity, including a derived half-sparsity condition for stability across all geometries (r1-r3).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Nested features are unstable except at perfect alignment, rather than generally forming stable overlapping directions (r4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The SAE passes the tested necessary pairwise and residual conditions on its training data, but those checks do not establish that its features are complete or canonical (r5-r6, r17).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Pairwise or residual optimality conditions fail in some shifted layers and code settings, showing that the extracted representation is not uniformly stable across these evaluations (r7-r8, r11-r12, r15-r16, r19, r21).
